notes.1c: Carbon dioxide and ammonia were occasionally seen.
notes.1d: to (h) These parts were answered extremely well.
notes.1i: This was answered less well. Oxygen was commonly seen.
notes.2a: This was answered reasonably well. Candidates occasionally stated the meaning of electrolysis rather than electrolyte. It is advisable for candidates to start their answer with, ‘An electrolyte is a substance….’. The fact that electrolytes contain ions or are ionic substances was omitted on occasions, as was the fact that electrolytes are aqueous or molten.
notes.2b: (i) Many responses did not include observations. Copper was often described as black or blue. The description of copper as a metal as opposed to a solid was seen occasionally. The word precipitate was occasionally incorrectly used as a description of copper. Copper was sometimes incorrectly named as copper(II).
notes.2bii: This straightforward question was poorly answered. H− was occasionally seen rather than H+, as was H rather than H . The equation was sometimes unbalanced.
notes.2iii: The ability to conduct electricity is among the most important requisite of any material used as an electrode; this was often omitted. Those that referred to conductivity sometimes omitted the term electrical or electricity. Some candidates suggested that an electrode should not be able to conduct electricity. Inertness was more commonly stated; others mentioned low reactivity, which was insufficient to gain credit.
notes.2iv: This was answered quite well. Ion was the most common incorrect answer. Copper was seen occasionally.
notes.3c: This was answered quite well. The higher percentage of lead was sometimes incompletely stated as a reason. More lead (unqualified) or higher yield were both insufficient to gain credit.
notes.3d: This was answered quite well. The most common error was to include oxygen as a reactant. The formula of lead(II) carbonate was occasionally seen as Pb(CO ) . 3 2
notes.3e: Only a minority of candidates performed well here. The formulae of lead(II) nitrate and/or nitric acid were commonly incorrect. Carbon dioxide was sometimes omitted as a product. Hydrogen was occasionally seen as a product.
notes.3f: (i) This was done reasonably well. Double bonds were sometimes absent.
notes.3fii: Those who realised that lead(II) oxide was ionic, sometimes contradicted this by referring to intermolecular forces or bonds between atoms or between ions and electrons. Many stated that covalent bonds are weak. Only a few candidates referred to forces of attraction between molecules in carbon dioxide.
notes.3g: Very few wrote a correct ionic equation for Experiment 1. Candidates would benefit from more practice with ionic equations. Most were correct in writing no reaction for Experiment 2.
notes.3h: (i) This was answered quite well. A common error was to refer to a burning splint relighting.
notes.3hii: Candidates found this to be extremely challenging. Nitrogen was the most common wrong answer. Ammonia was occasionally seen.
notes.4b: This was answered quite well. Silicon(IV) oxide was the most common incorrect answer.
notes.4c: (i) This was answered quite well; others left this unanswered or omitted to use the Avogadro constant. Some multiplied the Avogadro constant by 22 without calculating the number of moles.
notes.4cii: Candidates found this challenging. 24 dm3 was rarely used to calculate the number of moles.
notes.5a: (i) Candidates found this challenging. Reference to either colour or end-point was expected.
notes.5aii: This was answered well. Phenolphthalein or methyl orange were the most commonly correct acid base indicators. Potassium manganate(VII) was a common incorrect answer.
notes.5b: Candidates found this challenging. Some described the titration being carried out despite being instructed not to. Several mentioned removing the indicator by fractional distillation. Many described heating but omitted to mention when to stop. Many omitted leaving the solution to crystallise. Drying was often mentioned without a description of how it should be done.
notes.5c: (i) This was answered reasonably well. Orange was the most common incorrect answer.
notes.5cii: Candidates found this the most challenging question on the paper. Answers given were only occasionally observations. Many confused this with the test for copper(II) ions using aqueous sodium hydroxide and described a blue precipitate, which either dissolved in excess or remained insoluble.
notes.5iii: This was answered quite well. Evolution of sulfur dioxide was occasionally mentioned.
notes.6b: (i) Candidates found this very challenging. Those that mentioned the evolution of oxygen gas sometimes omitted to mention that the gas escaped from the flask. Many candidates did not understand the principle of conservation of mass, suggesting that the loss in mass was due to all of the reactants being used up. Loss of mass can only occur if matter escapes from the flask. Many suggested that the rate becomes constant (instead of the rate becoming zero) when the graph levels off.
notes.6bii: The key to answering this question correctly was to realise that the rate is highest at the start, decreases as time increases and then becomes zero because the reaction stops. Some candidates stated that the rate increased and some added that this was because a catalyst is present. The command word ‘describe’ is different in its requirements to ‘explain’. Although many responses referred to collision theory, this was unnecessary in a ‘describe’ question.
notes.6c: (i) Most candidates realised that the particles gain energy at a higher temperature, which leads to a greater collision frequency. Far fewer candidates referred to a greater proportion of molecules having enough energy to react when they collide. Some stated that more collisions occur without reference to frequency or time.
notes.6cii: This was answered reasonably well. The graph should have been steep at the start (because the rate is larger) and level off at the same mass (because the same amount of oxygen is evolved).
notes.7a: This was answered reasonably well. Some candidates stated ‘same molecular formula’ or ‘same structures’. Some answers were vague.
notes.7b: (i) This was answered reasonably well. Polymerisation was a common incorrect answer.
notes.7bii: Ethene was often missing from the products. The requirement to read the question carefully should be stressed repeatedly. Some formulae, e.g. C H , were unviable molecules. Ethene was often 3 7 represented as C H . 4 8
notes.7iii: This was answered quite well. A section of a polymer should never have brackets with or without an n subscript. Some candidates only drew one repeat unit. Extension bonds were sometimes missing.
notes.7iv: This was answered quite well. Names of other industrial processes were occasionally seen.
notes.7v: Conditions were often vague, e.g. high temperature or pressure. Some thought steam was a condition.
notes.7c: Candidates found this challenging. Vague answers such as less pollution / renewable resources / more environmentally friendly / less waste / cheaper were much more common than anything specific.
notes.7d: (i) This was answered quite well. Addition, halogenation and displacement were seen occasionally.
notes.7dii: This was answered quite well. Condensation and additional were the most common wrong answers.
notes.7e: Candidates found this challenging. Those who drew a carboxylic acid group often missed out the O-H bond.
notes.key_messages:
• There were many excellent papers seen.
• Candidates consistently make mistakes in writing and balancing chemical equations. The main problem
was a lack of knowledge of chemical formulae.

notes.general_comments:
Candidates have difficulties with questions that ask them to state the observations or to say what they would
see when an experiment is performed. It is unnecessary to give names of substances in answer to such
questions. Points that should be essential parts of the answers to such questions are:
• colours and changes in colour
• effervescence
• solids dissolving or disappearing
• precipitates forming.
